sections.history: Thirumullaivasal stands on the Coromandel coast of the Kaveri delta, only a short walk from the sea, and the Tevaram knows it as Then-Tirumullaivayil, the southern Tirumullaivayil, to tell it apart from its namesake in the Tondai country near Chennai. The saint Tirugnanasambandar praised the Lord of this place in a decad of the Tevaram, and tradition counts it among the shrines north of the Kaveri visited and sung by the saints, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam. Local tradition credits the first shrine to the early Chola king Killivalavan, and the temple is said to have been rebuilt in stone under the later Cholas. Its present form owes much to later renewal, and a consecration ceremony was held here in 1989. Worship has gone on here for well over a thousand years.
sections.architecture: The temple is entered through a modest arched gateway rather than a towering gopuram, which suits its quiet setting near the shore. Within the enclosure the sanctum of Mullaivananathar holds a self-manifested Shiva linga, about three and a half feet tall, and the goddess Anikonda Kothai Ammai, also called Satyananda Soundari, is honoured in her own shrine. The courtyard carries smaller shrines to Vinayaka, Murugan, Bhairava, the Nayanmar, Vishnu, Durga, Mahalakshmi and the Navagrahas. The temple is associated with four sacred waters, the theerthams of Vishnu, Chandra, Brahma and Ganga, and the jasmine, or mullai, creeper is honoured as the sacred tree of the place.
sections.legends: The legend of the temple belongs to Killivalavan, a Chola king and, in the telling, the grandfather of Karikala. Afflicted by a skin disease, he was advised by his physicians to bathe at a revered Shiva shrine, and he came to this shore to bathe in the sea. As he rode through the thicket his horse's legs were caught in dense mullai creepers, and when he struck at them with his sword the blade fell on a hidden Shiva linga, which bled. Stricken, the king prayed, and the Lord appeared to him and healed him. The mark of the blow is said to remain on the linga, and from the mullai creepers the place took its name, Tirumullaivayil, and the Lord that of Mullaivananathar, Lord of the jasmine forest.
sections.festivals: The great festival of the temple is the Masi Magam Theerthavari, in February or March, when the festival images of Mullaivananathar and the goddess are carried in procession to the seashore for the sacred sea-bath, which draws devotees from the surrounding villages. Thai Poosam in January or February, Masi Shivaratri and Avani Vinayaka Chaturthi are also observed, and the monthly Pradosham is kept as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Then-Tirumullaivayil is a place for those who like to travel slowly. The road from Sirkazhi runs through fields and coconut groves towards the coast, and as you near the temple the air changes with the nearness of the sea. Enter by the arched gateway and come first to Mullaivananathar in the sanctum, then turn to the goddess Anikonda Kothai Ammai in her own shrine. Many devotees walk on to the seashore, where the sacred bath of Masi Magam is kept, and those who suffer from ailments of the skin pray here with particular faith, remembering the king who was healed. On an ordinary day the temple is quiet and unhurried, with the sound of the sea in the distance.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again in the late afternoon and evening, with a midday break; one listing gives 8:00 to 12:30 and 4:00 to 8:00, but confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Thirumullaivasal is about 14 km from Sirkazhi, 32 km from Chidambaram and 36 km from Mayiladuthurai, and the sea lies roughly half a kilometre from the temple. Sirkazhi, with buses on to the coast, is the nearest practical railway station, and Chidambaram and Mayiladuthurai are also on the main line. Local buses run from Sirkazhi, but a hired car or auto-rickshaw is the easiest way to reach the coast. Tiruchirappalli and Puducherry are the nearest airports, both some distance away.
